requirements.request: For a red blood cell whose membrane permits water movement but not movement of the relevant solutes, compare isotonic, hypertonic and hypotonic extracellular solutions
Describe net water movement and the resulting cell-volume changes. In an isotonic solution, does "no net water movement" mean individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane

requirement_fragments.exact_text: If the cell's osmolarity matches that of the extracellular fluid, there will be no net movement of water into or out of the cell, although water will still move in and out.

Left: A RBC placed in a hypotonic solution, where the concentration of solutes in the surrounding fluid is lower than those in the cell, will cause water to rush into the RBC and lead to lysis of the cell.
Middle: there is no net water movement into or out of the cell as the concentration of the solutes inside the cell equal or is isotonic to that of the surrounding fluid.

Right: a RBC placed in a hypertonic solution, where the concentration of solutes in the surrounding fluid is greater than that in the cell will cause water to rush out of the cell and into the surrounding fluid.

FIGURE 11.27 Red blood cell membranes are water permeable and will (a) swell and possibly rupture in a hypotonic solution; (b) maintain normal volume and shape in an isotonic solution; and (c) shrivel and possibly die in a hypertonic solution. Consequently, measuring one of these properties for a solution prepared using a known mass of solute permits determination of the solute’s molar mass. question: For a red blood cell whose membrane permits water movement but not movement of the relevant solutes, compare isotonic, hypertonic and hypotonic extracellular solutions. Describe net water movement and the resulting cell-volume changes. In an isotonic solution, does "no net water movement" mean individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane?
answer_text:
In an isotonic solution, there is no net water movement and the red blood cell retains its normal volume. [ev_004]

In a hypertonic solution, net water movement is out of the cell and the cell shrinks. [ev_003]

In a hypotonic solution, net water movement is into the cell and the cell swells, potentially lysing. [ev_003]

In an isotonic solution, individual water molecules stop crossing the membrane. [ev_004]
